metadata.title: United States v. International Business MacHines Corp. Certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit, 517 U.S. 843 (1996) (No. 95-591)
metadata.creator: Supreme Court of the United States
metadata.description:
Case name: United States v. International Business MacHines Corp. Certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit

Opinion filed: 1996-06-10

Docket No.: 95-591

Citations:
• 135 L. Ed. 2d 124
• 116 S. Ct. 1793
• 517 U.S. 843
• 1996 U.S. LEXIS 3716

Case holding summaries:
• “It is simply no longer true that the Court perceives no substantive difference between the two Clauses.”
• “there is substantial evidence from the [Convention] Debates that proponents of the Clause fully intended the breadth of scope that is evident in the language”
• distinguishing the Art. I, § 9, cl. 5, Export Clause, which bars the United States from imposing any tax on exports, from the Import-Export Clause, which prohibits States from levying only duties and imposts
• reaffirming that Michelin expressly overruled the original package doctrine altogether and not merely Low on its facts
• distinguishing accommodations made under the Commerce Clause from the express textual prohibition of the Import-Export Clause
• interpreting Jones Act to allow action to be brought in admiralty
• imposition of legacy taxes in the same 1797 statute casts doubt on claim that Congress lacks such power
• delivery to common carrier signals commencement of export
• "where a statute is susceptible of two constructions, by one of which grave and doubtful constitutional questions arise and by the other of which such questions are avoided, our duty is to adopt the latter"
• compliance with the Import-Export Clause may be secured "by prohibiting the assessment of even nondiscriminatory property taxes on [import or export] goods which are merely in transit through the State when the tax is assessed"
• "It was not the purpose of the commerce clause to relieve those engaged in interstate commerce from their just share of state tax burden even though it increases the cost of doing the business"
• addressing a theory not argued by the parties but advanced by Justice Thomas in dissent
• "even an explicit concession" by the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico that it was subject to the requirements of the Fourth Amendment would not "relieve this Court of the per-formance of the judicial function of deciding the issue"
• "The [Alien Enemy Act of 1798] is almost as old as the Constitution, and it would savor of doctrinaire audacity now to find the statute offensive to some emanation of the Bill of Rights"
• overturning Swift v. Tyson , 16 Pet. 1 (1842), as unconstitutional
• the Court declined to overrule a case because it had "been controlling precedent for over 80 years."
• finding that party abandoned issue by failing to address it in the party’s brief on the merits
• holding that the United States Constitution does not permit the imposition of a generally applicable, nondiscriminatory federal tax on goods in export transit
• rejecting the government's argument that the Commerce, Import-Export and Export Clauses should be read in harmony to permit the imposition of generally applicable, nondiscriminatory taxes on exports
• rejecting government's request to "reinterpret the Export Clause to permit the imposition of generally applicable, nondiscriminatory taxes as [the Court has] under the Commerce Clause...."
• "While the original impetus may have had a narrow focus, the remedial provision that ultimately became the Export Clause does not, and there is substantial evidence from the Debates that proponents of the Clause fully intended the breadth of scope that is evident in the language."
• holding that "[i]t would be inappropriate for us to [e]xamine in this case, without the benefit of the parties' briefing," an issue the Government had conceded
• "The text of the Export Clause, on the other hand, expressly prohibits Congress from laying any tax or duty on exports."
• when a party "cho[o]se[s] not to" pursue a legal theory potentially available to it on appeal, we generally take the position that it is "inappropriate. . . without the benefit of the parties' briefing" to pursue that theory in our opinions
• holding it "clear that the Export Clause strictly prohibits any tax or duty, discriminatory or not, that falls on exports during the course of exportation"
• "We have good reason to hesitate before adopting the analysis of our recent Import-Export Clause cases into our Export Clause jurisprudence. . . . [M]eaningful textual differences exist [between the two Clauses] and should not be overlooked."
• chronicling the rise and fall of the "original package" doctrine
• "It would be inappropriate for us to []examine ... without the benefit of the parties' briefing," matters that a party has chosen not to contest.
• "Though we have frequently interpreted the Clauses together . . . our more recent . . . cases . . . caution that meaningful textual differences should not be overlooked."
